documents.title: What retrieval-augmented generation is
documents.text: Retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG, is a technique that gives a language model access to outside documents when it answers a question. Instead of relying only on what the model memorised during training, the system first searches a collection of documents for passages related to the question. Those passages are placed in the prompt, and the model is asked to write its answer using them. Because the answer is built from retrieved text, the system can point back to the sources it used.

documents.title: Why grounding reduces made-up answers
documents.text: Language models sometimes produce statements that sound confident but are wrong, which is often called hallucination. Grounding the model in retrieved passages lowers the chance of this, because the model can copy or paraphrase facts that are actually in front of it. Grounding does not remove the problem completely. A model can still misread a passage or add details that the passage does not contain, so many systems add a fact-checking step that compares each claim with the passage it cites.

documents.title: How documents are prepared for search
documents.text: Before documents can be searched, they are cleaned and split into short chunks, often a few hundred words long. Neighbouring chunks usually overlap a little so that an idea that crosses a boundary is not lost. Each chunk is then turned into an embedding, which is a list of numbers that captures its meaning. The embeddings are stored in a vector database together with details such as the source address and the publication date.

documents.title: Finding the most relevant passages
documents.text: To answer a question, the system embeds the question in the same way and looks for the chunks whose embeddings are closest to it, commonly measured with cosine similarity. For topics that change quickly, such as news, the ranking can also favour recent items. For background explanations, it can instead favour sources that are known to be authoritative. The best few passages are then handed to the model.
documents.text_v2: To answer a question, the system embeds the question in the same way and looks for the chunks whose embeddings are closest to it, commonly measured with cosine similarity. For topics that change quickly, such as news, the ranking can also favour recent items. For background explanations, it can instead favour sources that are known to be authoritative. Many systems then rerank the top results with a second model, which can improve the quality of the final passages. The best few passages are then handed to the model.

documents.title: Citing sources in the answer
documents.text: A grounded answer is more useful when it shows where each statement came from. Systems do this by attaching a reference to every factual claim that points to the passage it was based on. A reader or a reviewer can then open the original source and check the claim. If a claim has no supporting passage, a careful system either removes it or marks it as unsupported.

documents.title: Sourdough starter basics (off-topic on purpose)
documents.text: A sourdough starter is a mixture of flour and water that collects wild yeast and bacteria. Feeding it regularly with fresh flour keeps it active. Bakers use a small amount of starter to make bread rise instead of commercial yeast.
